topic.title: The hospital estimate nobody believes
topic.claim: We pay hospital bills like hostages because we don't know what anything should cost and we're too scared to ask in the middle of a crisis.
topic.behaviour: People sign consent forms and estimates without scrutiny, then watch the final bill climb and settle just to be discharged.
topic.mechanism: Fear plus information asymmetry. When someone you love is in pain, haggling feels like gambling with their care, so we pay and tell the story later.
topic.group: urban families who have had a hospital stay

paragraphs: You'll fight an auto driver over the fare. Then sign a hospital estimate without reading one line. Where does that fight go?
It goes to the corridor outside the ward. Someone you love is on a bed inside.
The billing desk has the pen and the file. Asking why it costs this much feels like a risk to their care.
Take one Bengaluru patient's account. A planned leg-implant removal, estimated at about ₹1.7 lakh.
The bill, they say, rose toward ₹2.33 lakh. Then came the condition: pay about ₹2.08 lakh, or no discharge.
It's not one bad hospital. In a LocalCircles survey, only 28% of people with a recently hospitalised family member said the bill listed every charge.
38% said many charges were lumped together. Good luck questioning a lump.
The same patient says staff scribbled a ₹15k discount on paper.
So there was room all along. The first number was just what you'd pay if you stayed quiet.
There is a rule on paper. The Health Ministry has asked states to make hospitals display rates.
People in the field doubt they do, and final bills can still drift.
Every family has a hospital bill story, told years later at dinner, with the exact number.
Almost none has a story about asking for the breakdown.

hook_candidates.hook: You'll fight an auto driver over the fare. Then sign a hospital estimate without reading one line. Where does that fight go?
A Bengaluru hospital quoted about ₹1.7 lakh for a leg operation. The bill crept toward ₹2.33 lakh. So why didn't anyone ask why?
Most Indian families pay hospital bills like hostages. And I know how that sounds.
Only 28% of families said their hospital bill listed every charge. Everyone else paid it anyway. Nobody asked a single question.
We don't skip questioning hospital bills because we trust the hospital. We skip it because someone we love is still on that bed.
